Frequency-Calibrated Decision-Focused Learning for BESS Dispatch Under Renewable Uncertainty

Zihan Meng    Chenxi Hu    Xin Cui    and Francis Yunhe Hou ††thanks: Z. Meng, X. Cui, and F. Y. Hou are with the Department of Electrical & Computer Engineering, The University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong.††thanks: C. Hu is with the Department of Computer Science, The Hang Seng University of Hong Kong, Hong Kong.
Abstract

Battery energy storage system (BESS) flexibility depends on state of charge and intertemporal operating constraints. Renewable forecast errors of similar magnitudes can lead to different BESS dispatch results. An error may alter early charging or discharging decisions and reduce the flexibility available for subsequent regulation, while another may have little effect on the resulting schedule. To account for these unequal consequences, this paper proposes Frequency-Calibrated Decision-Focused Learning (FC-DFL), which trains renewable predictors using the realized operating costs of their induced BESS schedules. Gaussian smoothing and solver-based zeroth-order estimation provide training feedback without requiring differentiating through the non-differentiable mixed-integer BESS dispatch problem. The same decision feedback is further combined with prediction sensitivity to develop a decision-oriented XAI method that identifies the input features and forecast periods most consequential to BESS operation. Case studies using German wind and solar data show that FC-DFL reduces the integrated absolute frequency-deviation metric by 6.05% and decision regret by 23.92% relative to accuracy-based predict-then-optimize method. The XAI analysis further demonstrates that the identified high-impact forecast periods produce 2.84 times larger average absolute changes in realized operating cost than low-impact periods. These findings highlight the importance of incorporating downstream decision-making outcomes into renewable forecasting and demonstrate the value of FC-DFL in improving BESS regulation and providing operationally meaningful forecast explanations.

Index Terms: 
Battery energy storage system, decision-focused learning, explainable artificial intelligence, frequency regulation, renewable forecasting, renewable uncertainty.

I Introduction

The increasing integration of wind and solar generation introduces greater variability and uncertainty into power-system operation. Renewable ramps change balancing requirements over different time scales, and forecast errors cause deviations between scheduled and realized renewable generation [1, 2, 3]. These errors may also be correlated across consecutive intervals, affecting operating decisions over an extended horizon. Accurate renewable forecasting is therefore important for generation scheduling, reserve allocation, and energy storage operation. However, forecast uncertainty cannot be eliminated, and its operating consequences depend on how the resulting predictions are used.

Renewable forecasting methods are commonly trained and evaluated using statistical measures such as mean squared error (MSE), root mean squared error (RMSE), and mean absolute error (MAE). These metrics measure forecast accuracy but do not directly quantify its value in downstream operation [1, 4]. Pinson et al. [5] demonstrated how probabilistic wind power forecasts can improve trading decisions by accounting for forecast uncertainty. Xie et al. [6] integrated spatiotemporal wind forecasts into robust look-ahead dispatch and quantified the resulting operating cost benefits. More broadly, Bertsimas and Kallus [7] developed a data-driven framework for making decisions from contextual information rather than treating prediction as an isolated task. These studies establish the importance of evaluating forecasts through their applications. For a constrained energy storage resource, however, the value of a forecast also depends on the physical operating conditions under which its predicted trajectory is used.

Battery energy storage systems (BESSs) provide flexibility through rapid charging and discharging and can support power balancing and frequency regulation [8]. Practical applications have demonstrated these capabilities. For example, the Hornsdale Power Reserve has provided frequency-control ancillary services in the Australian electricity market [9]. He et al. [10] developed a coordinated wind–battery regulation strategy and examined its participation in energy and regulation markets. Xu et al. [11] further investigated battery control and bidding for frequency regulation, considering operating performance and battery aging. These studies highlight the importance of coordinating battery operation with regulation requirements. The available BESS response also depends on state of charge (SOC), charging and discharging power, ramp limits, and the energy required in subsequent intervals [12].

The same operating constraints also affect the consequences of renewable forecast errors. BESS dispatch is determined from a renewable forecast, while its realized regulation performance depends on the renewable generation that actually occurs. Forecasts with similar error magnitudes can induce different charging and discharging schedules and SOC trajectories, leading to different realized costs. An earlier BESS decision changes the stored energy available in subsequent intervals, while power and ramp limits further restrict the feasible dispatch trajectory. Pointwise forecasting losses do not capture these intertemporal operating consequences, motivating the use of realized decision cost in predictor training.

Decision-focused learning (DFL) offers a means of aligning prediction with optimization. Task-based learning incorporates downstream objectives into model training [13], and subsequent approaches have developed methods for learning from optimization decisions [14]. Smart Predict-then-Optimize (SPO) formalizes decision-based prediction losses for problems with uncertain objective coefficients [15]. Related developments have also addressed uncertainty beyond the objective. Estes and Richard [16] studied SPO for two-stage linear programs with uncertain right-hand-side parameters, and Mandi et al. [17] examined feasibility and decision quality when optimization constraints contain predicted parameters. These advances demonstrate that DFL can address different forms of optimization uncertainty. Its application nevertheless requires a training signal consistent with the physical role of the predicted quantities and the downstream optimizer.

Recent research has also incorporated DFL into energy storage applications. Yi et al. [18] developed a perturbation-based DFL framework for linear storage models, with applications to energy arbitrage and storage behavior prediction. Kim et al. [19] proposed a neural optimizer that integrates forecasting and BESS control for electricity cost and peak-demand management. These studies demonstrate the potential of decision-focused methods in storage operation. For BESS regulation under renewable uncertainty, renewable generation enters the native power-balance constraint as a physical injection, while BESS dispatch includes binary charging/discharging decisions and intertemporal SOC constraints. The canonical SPO+ surrogate assumes uncertain objective coefficients over a fixed feasible set and does not directly accommodate renewable generation entering the native power-balance right-hand side. Furthermore, gradients obtained through a continuous storage relaxation do not directly capture the exact mixed-integer BESS decisions. The resulting training signal must therefore reflect the realized cost of forecast-induced BESS dispatch without requiring derivatives of the mixed-integer optimizer.

The distinction between prediction sensitivity and realized BESS operating cost is also important for model interpretability. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) has been increasingly studied in power and energy systems to improve the transparency of machine-learning models [20]. For solar forecasting, Mitrentsis and Lens [21] used SHAP to interpret point forecasts and prediction intervals. Liao et al. [22] investigated several XAI techniques for wind power forecasting and evaluated the reliability of their feature explanations. These approaches provide insight into how predictor inputs affect forecast outputs. For BESS regulation, however, a feature with high prediction importance does not necessarily have a large effect on realized operating cost. Conversely, a smaller forecast change can be important when it alters BESS decisions across constrained operating intervals. This distinction calls for explanations that connect prediction sensitivity with downstream BESS operation.

To address these challenges, this paper proposes Frequency-Calibrated Decision-Focused Learning (FC-DFL) for renewable forecasting and BESS regulation. FC-DFL uses the realized cost of forecast-induced BESS dispatch to connect predictor training with decision-oriented interpretation. The main contributions of FC-DFL are summarized as follows.

  1. 1.

    We develop a decision-focused renewable forecasting model for BESS regulation. FC-DFL evaluates the BESS schedules induced by renewable forecasts under realized renewable generation. The resulting decision cost captures the effects of forecast errors on intertemporal BESS operation and the regulation capability available in subsequent intervals.

  2. 2.

    We develop an RHS-compatible decision-focused training method for mixed-integer BESS dispatch. FC-DFL employs Gaussian smoothing and solver-based zeroth-order estimation to obtain decision gradients from realized operating costs. The smoothed-gradient identity and conditional unbiasedness of the estimators are established under explicit assumptions. The resulting feedback enables predictor training without differentiating through the BESS optimizer.

  3. 3.

    We develop a decision-oriented XAI method using the same time-resolved decision gradient as FC-DFL training. By combining this feedback with the predictor Jacobian, the method identifies input features and forecast periods with greater importance to realized BESS operation. Matched perturbation tests using the exact BESS dispatch model validate the operational relevance of the importance rankings.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II develops the physical BESS regulation model and realized decision cost. Section III presents FC-DFL training. Section IV introduces decision-oriented explainability. Section V reports the case studies. Section VI concludes the paper.

II Forecast-Coupled BESS Regulation Model

Renewable forecast errors affect BESS regulation through the operating decisions they induce. This section first describes renewable variability and forecast uncertainty, then formulates the intertemporal BESS constraints. The resulting model establishes how renewable forecasts determine BESS dispatch and its realized operating cost. The overall framework of FC-DFL is illustrated in Fig. 1.

II-A Renewable Variability and Forecast Errors

Let 𝒯={1,…,T}\mathcal{T}=\{1,\ldots,T\} denote the dispatch intervals, each of duration Δ​t\Delta t. Wind and photovoltaic (PV) generation exhibit variations over different time scales. Renewable ramps are commonly characterized by their magnitude, rate, duration, and direction [23, 24, 2]. For sample ii, the aggregate renewable generation and its variation over τ\tau intervals are expressed as

ri,t\displaystyle r_{i,t} =ri,tw+ri,tpv,t∈𝒯,\displaystyle=r_{i,t}^{\mathrm{w}}+r_{i,t}^{\mathrm{pv}},\qquad t\in\mathcal{T}, (1a)
Δτ​ri,t\displaystyle\Delta_{\tau}r_{i,t} =ri,t−ri,t−τ,t=τ+1,…,T.\displaystyle=r_{i,t}-r_{i,t-\tau},\qquad t=\tau+1,\ldots,T. (1b)

The renewable change Δτ​ri,t\Delta_{\tau}r_{i,t} captures both the magnitude and direction of a ramp over τ​Δ​t\tau\Delta t. Its average ramp rate follows from the change per unit time. These characteristics describe the renewable power trajectory, but they do not determine the regulation effort required from the BESS. That effort also depends on the available charging and discharging capability when the variation occurs.

Forecast uncertainty introduces a further difference between scheduled and realized renewable generation. Following the forecast-minus-realization convention [25], the forecast errors and conventional squared-error loss are given by

ϵi,t\displaystyle\epsilon_{i,t} =r^i,t−ri,t,\displaystyle=\hat{r}_{i,t}-r_{i,t}, (2a)
ϵi\displaystyle\bm{\epsilon}_{i} =𝒓^i−𝒓i,\displaystyle=\hat{\bm{r}}_{i}-\bm{r}_{i}, (2b)
ϵi,t,τramp\displaystyle\epsilon_{i,t,\tau}^{\mathrm{ramp}} =Δτ​r^i,t−Δτ​ri,t=ϵi,t−ϵi,t−τ,\displaystyle=\Delta_{\tau}\hat{r}_{i,t}-\Delta_{\tau}r_{i,t}=\epsilon_{i,t}-\epsilon_{i,t-\tau}, (2c)
ℒiMSE\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{i}^{\mathrm{MSE}} =1T​‖ϵi‖22.\displaystyle=\frac{1}{T}\left\|\bm{\epsilon}_{i}\right\|_{2}^{2}. (2d)

The error ϵi,t\epsilon_{i,t} measures the renewable mismatch at one interval, whereas ϵi,t,τramp\epsilon_{i,t,\tau}^{\mathrm{ramp}} measures the error in renewable change across two intervals. MSE aggregates squared forecast errors without accounting for their temporal ordering. Consequently, forecasts with the same MSE can distribute their errors differently across the dispatch horizon. The resulting operating consequences depend on the BESS state and constraints, as developed next.

II-B BESS Regulation Model

BESS regulation is constrained by the available converter power, stored energy, and intertemporal operating limits. Let ziz_{i} collect the charging and discharging powers, net BESS power, binary operating modes, and SOC trajectory over the TT-interval horizon. Positive pi,tbessp_{i,t}^{\mathrm{bess}} denotes net discharge to the system. The rated power P¯\bar{P} is reduced by the retained headroom PresP^{\mathrm{res}}, leaving PuseP^{\mathrm{use}} available for the modeled dispatch.

The BESS operating constraints are

|pi,tbess−pi,t−1bess|\displaystyle\left|p_{i,t}^{\mathrm{bess}}-p_{i,t-1}^{\mathrm{bess}}\right| ≤Rbess​Δ​t,t∈𝒯∪{T+1}.\displaystyle\leq R^{\mathrm{bess}}\Delta t,\quad t\in\mathcal{T}\cup\{T+1\}. (3j)

The binary operating mode enforces mutually exclusive charging and discharging. The SOC dynamics in (3f) account for conversion losses and couple BESS decisions across consecutive intervals. The terminal SOC condition prevents artificial energy depletion over the scheduling horizon, while (3i) and (3j) constrain power changes at both scheduling boundaries.

These constraints make the available BESS response dependent on its operating trajectory. A high SOC provides more energy for discharging but less capacity to absorb renewable surplus, while a low SOC has the opposite effect. Previous BESS power and the remaining scheduling horizon further restrict admissible actions. Thus, similar renewable variations can require different corrective schedules depending on when they occur. The complete set of physical trajectories satisfying (3) is denoted by 𝒳iBESS\mathcal{X}_{i}^{\mathrm{BESS}}. This set includes the binary operating modes, SOC dynamics, power limits, ramp constraints, and terminal condition. It is fixed with respect to the renewable forecast. Forecast changes affect the selected BESS trajectory, rather than the underlying physical constraints.

II-C Forecast-Coupled Dispatch and Realized Decision Cost

Renewable forecasts determine BESS dispatch through the power-balance requirement. Let pi,tloadp_{i,t}^{\mathrm{load}} denote the exogenous balance requirement presented to the renewable–BESS regulation layer after accounting for scheduled non-BESS supply. It remains fixed between forecast-driven dispatch and realized evaluation, so renewable generation is the only uncertain quantity considered in the regulation problem.

For a generic renewable trajectory 𝝆=[ρ1,…,ρT]⊤\bm{\rho}=[\rho_{1},\ldots,\rho_{T}]^{\top}, the residual imbalance and forecast-coupled BESS optimization problem are formulated as

ei,t​(zi,𝝆)\displaystyle e_{i,t}(z_{i};\bm{\rho}) =pi,tnet​(𝝆)−pi,tbess,\displaystyle=p_{i,t}^{\mathrm{net}}(\bm{\rho})-p_{i,t}^{\mathrm{bess}}, (4b)
Δ​fi,t\displaystyle\Delta f_{i,t} =−ei,t​(zi,𝝆)Bsys,\displaystyle=-\frac{e_{i,t}(z_{i};\bm{\rho})}{B^{\mathrm{sys}}}, (4c)
κ\displaystyle\kappa =1+λfBsys,\displaystyle=1+\frac{\lambda_{f}}{B^{\mathrm{sys}}}, (4d)
Ψi​(zi,𝝆)\displaystyle\Psi_{i}(z_{i};\bm{\rho}) =Δt∑t=1T[κ|ei,t(zi;𝝆)|\displaystyle=\Delta t\sum_{t=1}^{T}\Big[\kappa\left|e_{i,t}(z_{i};\bm{\rho})\right|
+λp(pi,tch+pi,tdch)],\displaystyle\qquad+\lambda_{p}\left(p_{i,t}^{\mathrm{ch}}+p_{i,t}^{\mathrm{dch}}\right)\Big], (4e)

The residual in (4b) represents the power imbalance remaining after renewable generation and BESS regulation. A positive residual indicates a power deficit and therefore corresponds to a negative frequency deviation. The relation in (4c) provides a quasi-steady approximation rather than a model of transient frequency dynamics. The operating objective combines absolute residual imbalance with a throughput penalty on BESS charging and discharging. The residual and frequency-referenced penalties are incorporated into κ\kappa, while λp\lambda_{p} regularizes BESS activity without representing electrochemical degradation. Minimizing (4e) over 𝒳iBESS\mathcal{X}_{i}^{\mathrm{BESS}} determines the physical BESS schedule induced by the renewable trajectory.

In the native mixed-integer formulation, renewable generation enters the right-hand side of the power-balance equation. Introducing nonnegative deficit and surplus variables gives the equivalent representation

+λp(pi,tch+pi,tdch)]\displaystyle\qquad+\lambda_{p}\left(p_{i,t}^{\mathrm{ch}}+p_{i,t}^{\mathrm{dch}}\right)\Big] (5c)

The deficit and surplus variables account for the remaining power imbalance in opposite directions. Unlike the reduced formulation, the native model places the renewable trajectory explicitly in the balance constraint. The two representations nevertheless produce the same optimal physical BESS dispatch, as established below.

Proposition 1

For any renewable trajectory 𝛒\bm{\rho} and fixed physical BESS action zi∈𝒳iBESSz_{i}\in\mathcal{X}_{i}^{\mathrm{BESS}}, the optimal deficit and surplus variables in (5) satisfy

The operating consequence of a forecast is determined by evaluating its induced BESS schedule under realized renewable generation. The realized decision cost, realization-aware reference, decision regret, and frequency-deviation metric are defined by

IAFDi​(zi)\displaystyle\mathrm{IAFD}_{i}(z_{i}) =Δ​tBsys​∑t=1T|pi,tload−ri,t−pi,tbess|.\displaystyle=\frac{\Delta t}{B^{\mathrm{sys}}}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\left|p_{i,t}^{\mathrm{load}}-r_{i,t}-p_{i,t}^{\mathrm{bess}}\right|. (7e)

The realized cost Fi​(𝝆)F_{i}(\bm{\rho}) evaluates the forecast-induced BESS dispatch under realized renewable generation. The resulting imbalance is recomputed using 𝒓i\bm{r}_{i}, while the physical BESS dispatch remains unchanged. The realization-aware reference instead optimizes directly with 𝒓i\bm{r}_{i} under the same physical constraints and exogenous balance requirement. It therefore provides the minimum realized cost for that sample. Since zi⋆​(𝝆)∈𝒳iBESSz_{i}^{\star}(\bm{\rho})\in\mathcal{X}_{i}^{\mathrm{BESS}}, the decision regret in (7d) is nonnegative. The IAFD in (7e) separately quantifies the accumulated magnitude of realized frequency deviations. For a fixed BESS action, the difference between the realized and forecast residuals equals ϵi,t\epsilon_{i,t}. However, changing the renewable forecast also changes the optimized BESS schedule over the entire horizon. Consequently, forecast errors with similar magnitudes can induce different charging and discharging decisions, SOC trajectories, and realized costs. This distinction links renewable forecast uncertainty to the intertemporal BESS constraints. Pointwise forecast accuracy does not account for the operating consequences of the induced schedule. The FC-DFL method developed in Section III therefore trains the renewable predictor using the realized decision cost in (7a).

III Frequency-Calibrated Decision-Focused Learning

The BESS model in Section II shows that renewable forecast errors affect realized regulation performance through the dispatch they induce. FC-DFL incorporates this operating consequence into predictor training. Gaussian smoothing provides a differentiable surrogate of the realized decision cost, while zeroth-order estimation obtains its gradient without differentiating through the mixed-integer BESS optimizer.

III-A Gaussian-Smoothed Realized Decision Cost

Unlike the canonical cost-vector SPO formulation [15], renewable generation enters the BESS power-balance right-hand side. The equivalent residual formulation in Section II-C allows forecast-induced dispatch to be evaluated over the fixed physical BESS feasible set. The realized decision cost in (7a) is evaluated using the exact forecast-induced BESS schedule. Since the optimizer contains binary operating decisions, its dependence on the renewable forecast need not be differentiable. FC-DFL instead smooths the realized decision cost evaluated at projected renewable forecasts.

Let ℛ⊂ℝT\mathcal{R}\subset\mathbb{R}^{T} be a nonempty, compact, and convex set of admissible renewable forecast trajectories, with Πℛ\Pi_{\mathcal{R}} denoting Euclidean projection onto this set. For 𝑼∼𝒩⁡(0,IT)\bm{U}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{T}) and σ>0\sigma>0, the predictor, projected cost, and smoothed decision objective are defined by

𝒓^i\displaystyle\hat{\bm{r}}_{i} =gθ​(𝒙i)∈ℝT,\displaystyle=g_{\theta}(\bm{x}_{i})\in\mathbb{R}^{T}, (8a)
F¯i​(𝒚)\displaystyle\bar{F}_{i}(\bm{y}) =Fi​(Πℛ​(𝒚)),𝒚∈ℝT,\displaystyle=F_{i}\left(\Pi_{\mathcal{R}}(\bm{y})\right),\quad\bm{y}\in\mathbb{R}^{T}, (8b)
F~i,σ​(𝝆)\displaystyle\widetilde{F}_{i,\sigma}(\bm{\rho}) =𝔼𝑼​[F¯i​(𝝆+σ​𝑼)],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\bm{U}}\left[\bar{F}_{i}(\bm{\rho}+\sigma\bm{U})\right], (8c)
ℓ~i,σdec​(𝝆)\displaystyle\widetilde{\ell}_{i,\sigma}^{\mathrm{dec}}(\bm{\rho}) =F~i,σ​(𝝆)−Fi​(𝒓i).\displaystyle=\widetilde{F}_{i,\sigma}(\bm{\rho})-F_{i}(\bm{r}_{i}). (8d)

Projection keeps forecast perturbations within ℛ\mathcal{R}, without altering the realized renewable trajectory 𝒓i\bm{r}_{i} used for cost evaluation and the reference. Because this reference cost is independent of the forecast, smoothing the decision regret gives the same gradient as smoothing FiF_{i}. The following assumptions establish the mathematical conditions required for this gradient.

Assumption 1

For every 𝛒∈ℛ\bm{\rho}\in\mathcal{R}, the BESS problem (4f) admits an optimal physical action. A fixed Borel-measurable selection rule determines zi⋆​(𝛒)z_{i}^{\star}(\bm{\rho}) when multiple optimal solutions exist.

Assumption 2

The restriction of the realized decision-cost function FiF_{i} to ℛ\mathcal{R} is bounded and Borel measurable.

Theorem 1

Under Assumptions 1 and 2, the smoothed decision cost F~i,σ\widetilde{F}_{i,\sigma} is infinitely differentiable on ℝT\mathbb{R}^{T} for every σ>0\sigma>0, with

∇𝝆F~i,σ​(𝝆)\displaystyle\nabla_{\bm{\rho}}\widetilde{F}_{i,\sigma}(\bm{\rho}) =1σ​𝔼𝑼​[F¯i​(𝝆+σ​𝑼)​𝑼].\displaystyle=\frac{1}{\sigma}\mathbb{E}_{\bm{U}}\left[\bar{F}_{i}(\bm{\rho}+\sigma\bm{U})\bm{U}\right]. (9)

Proof: The smoothed objective in (8c) is the convolution of the bounded measurable function F¯i\bar{F}_{i} with a Gaussian density. Every derivative of the Gaussian kernel is integrable, allowing differentiation under the integral. Differentiating with respect to 𝝆\bm{\rho} and expressing the result using 𝑼∼𝒩⁡(0,IT)\bm{U}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{T}) gives (9). The same argument applies to derivatives of higher orders. □\square

Theorem 1 provides a decision gradient without requiring derivatives of the mixed-integer optimizer. Evaluated at the renewable forecast, this time-resolved feedback is

giopt\displaystyle g_{i}^{\mathrm{opt}} =∇𝒓^iF~i,σ​(𝒓^i)∈ℝT.\displaystyle=\nabla_{\hat{\bm{r}}_{i}}\widetilde{F}_{i,\sigma}\left(\hat{\bm{r}}_{i}\right)\in\mathbb{R}^{T}. (10)

The component gi,toptg_{i,t}^{\mathrm{opt}} measures the sensitivity of the smoothed realized decision cost to the renewable forecast at interval tt. Unlike a fixed penalty on forecast error, this sensitivity reflects the BESS schedule obtained from the complete forecast trajectory and the realized operating cost it produces. At continuity points of F¯i\bar{F}_{i}, F~i,σ​(𝝆)\widetilde{F}_{i,\sigma}(\bm{\rho}) converges to F¯i​(𝝆)\bar{F}_{i}(\bm{\rho}) as σ→0\sigma\to 0.

III-B Zeroth-Order Decision Feedback

The gradient in (9) can be estimated from realized decision-cost evaluations obtained using the exact BESS optimizer. For independent directions 𝒖i,k∼𝒩⁡(0,IT)\bm{u}_{i,k}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I_{T}), k=1,…,Kk=1,\ldots,K, the one-sided and antithetic estimators are

g^i,oneopt\displaystyle\widehat{g}_{i,\mathrm{one}}^{\mathrm{opt}} =1K​σ∑k=1K[F¯i(𝒓^i+σ𝒖i,k)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{K\sigma}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\Big[\bar{F}_{i}\left(\hat{\bm{r}}_{i}+\sigma\bm{u}_{i,k}\right)
−F¯i(𝒓^i)]𝒖i,k,\displaystyle\qquad-\bar{F}_{i}\left(\hat{\bm{r}}_{i}\right)\Big]\bm{u}_{i,k}, (11a)
g^i,antiopt\displaystyle\widehat{g}_{i,\mathrm{anti}}^{\mathrm{opt}} =12​K​σ∑k=1K[F¯i(𝒓^i+σ𝒖i,k)\displaystyle=\frac{1}{2K\sigma}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\Big[\bar{F}_{i}\left(\hat{\bm{r}}_{i}+\sigma\bm{u}_{i,k}\right)
−F¯i(𝒓^i−σ𝒖i,k)]𝒖i,k.\displaystyle\qquad-\bar{F}_{i}\left(\hat{\bm{r}}_{i}-\sigma\bm{u}_{i,k}\right)\Big]\bm{u}_{i,k}. (11b)
Proposition 2

Under the conditions of Theorem 1, both estimators in (11) are conditionally unbiased for the same smoothed decision gradient:

𝔼[g^i,oneopt∣θ,𝒙i,𝒓i]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\widehat{g}_{i,\mathrm{one}}^{\mathrm{opt}}\mid\theta,\bm{x}_{i},\bm{r}_{i}\right] =giopt,\displaystyle=g_{i}^{\mathrm{opt}}, (12a)
𝔼[g^i,antiopt∣θ,𝒙i,𝒓i]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\left[\widehat{g}_{i,\mathrm{anti}}^{\mathrm{opt}}\mid\theta,\bm{x}_{i},\bm{r}_{i}\right] =giopt.\displaystyle=g_{i}^{\mathrm{opt}}. (12b)

Proof: Conditional on the current sample and predictor parameters, F¯i​(𝒓^i)\bar{F}_{i}(\hat{\bm{r}}_{i}) is fixed. Since 𝔼⁡[𝑼]=0\mathbb{E}[\bm{U}]=0, subtracting this baseline does not change the expected gradient. Theorem 1 therefore establishes (12a). For the antithetic estimator, the symmetry of the Gaussian distribution gives

𝔼⁡[F¯i​(𝒓^i−σ​𝑼)​𝑼]=−𝔼⁡[F¯i​(𝒓^i+σ​𝑼)​𝑼].\mathbb{E}\left[\bar{F}_{i}(\hat{\bm{r}}_{i}-\sigma\bm{U})\bm{U}\right]=-\mathbb{E}\left[\bar{F}_{i}(\hat{\bm{r}}_{i}+\sigma\bm{U})\bm{U}\right].

Substitution into (11b) yields (12b). □\square Each perturbed renewable forecast induces a BESS dispatch schedule whose realized cost reflects intertemporal SOC constraints and operating decisions. The resulting decision gradient provides feedback on BESS regulation performance rather than forecast accuracy alone. FC-DFL training uses the baseline-centered one-sided estimator, requiring K+1K+1 BESS optimizations per gradient estimate. The antithetic estimator estimates the same gradient and is used for decision-oriented analysis in Section IV.

III-C FC-DFL Predictor Training

The smoothed decision objective connects renewable forecasting with realized BESS regulation performance. For NN training samples, FC-DFL minimizes the average smoothed decision regret. The corresponding gradient and backpropagation surrogate are

ℒFC​(θ)\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FC}}(\theta) =1N​∑i=1Nℓ~i,σdec​(gθ​(𝒙i)),\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\widetilde{\ell}_{i,\sigma}^{\mathrm{dec}}\left(g_{\theta}(\bm{x}_{i})\right), (13a)
∇θℒFC​(θ)\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{FC}}(\theta) =1N​∑i=1N[∇θgθ​(𝒙i)]⊤​giopt,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\left[\nabla_{\theta}g_{\theta}(\bm{x}_{i})\right]^{\top}g_{i}^{\mathrm{opt}}, (13b)
ℒiback\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{i}^{\mathrm{back}} =⟨sg⁡(g^i,oneopt),𝒓^i⟩,\displaystyle=\left\langle\operatorname{sg}\left(\widehat{g}_{i,\mathrm{one}}^{\mathrm{opt}}\right),\hat{\bm{r}}_{i}\right\rangle, (13c)
∇θℒiback\displaystyle\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}_{i}^{\mathrm{back}} =[∇θgθ​(𝒙i)]⊤​g^i,oneopt.\displaystyle=\left[\nabla_{\theta}g_{\theta}(\bm{x}_{i})\right]^{\top}\widehat{g}_{i,\mathrm{one}}^{\mathrm{opt}}. (13d)

The predictor Jacobian combines with the decision gradient gioptg_{i}^{\mathrm{opt}}, allowing forecast periods to contribute according to their realized operating consequences. In implementation, the stochastic feedback g^i,oneopt\widehat{g}_{i,\mathrm{one}}^{\mathrm{opt}} replaces the expected gradient in this expression. The stop-gradient operator sg⁡(⋅)\operatorname{sg}(\cdot) in (13c) treats the solver feedback as fixed during backpropagation. Differentiating the surrogate therefore passes the estimated decision gradient through the renewable predictor without differentiating the mixed-integer BESS optimization problem. The resulting training procedure adjusts renewable forecasts according to the realized costs of their induced BESS schedules, rather than minimizing forecast MSE alone. Because the same gioptg_{i}^{\mathrm{opt}} is defined for each forecast interval, it also provides the optimization feedback used for decision-oriented interpretation in Section IV.

IV Decision-Oriented Explainability

The optimization feedback developed in Section III links renewable forecast changes to realized BESS operating cost. This section uses the same feedback to identify predictor inputs whose effects on renewable forecasts have greater downstream importance. The resulting importance scores are evaluated through matched perturbations and exact BESS reoptimization.

IV-A Decision-Oriented Feature Importance

Prediction sensitivity measures how an input feature affects renewable forecasts, but it does not account for the resulting BESS operating decisions. To incorporate the downstream consequence, consider the differentiable predictor gθg_{\theta} and the smoothed realized cost F~i,σ\widetilde{F}_{i,\sigma}. Their relationship is given by

Jipred\displaystyle J_{i}^{\mathrm{pred}} =∇𝒙igθ​(𝒙i)∈ℝT×d,\displaystyle=\nabla_{\bm{x}_{i}}g_{\theta}(\bm{x}_{i})\in\mathbb{R}^{T\times d}, (14a)
Gi,j,tpred\displaystyle G_{i,j,t}^{\mathrm{pred}} =|[Jipred]t,j|,\displaystyle=\left|\left[J_{i}^{\mathrm{pred}}\right]_{t,j}\right|, (14b)
Hi​(𝒙)\displaystyle H_{i}(\bm{x}) =F~i,σ​(gθ​(𝒙)),\displaystyle=\widetilde{F}_{i,\sigma}\left(g_{\theta}(\bm{x})\right), (14c)
∂Hi​(𝒙i)∂xi,j\displaystyle\frac{\partial H_{i}(\bm{x}_{i})}{\partial x_{i,j}} =∑t∈𝒯gi,topt​[Jipred]t,j.\displaystyle=\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}g_{i,t}^{\mathrm{opt}}\left[J_{i}^{\mathrm{pred}}\right]_{t,j}. (14d)

The predictor Jacobian captures the sensitivity of renewable forecasts to input features. In (14d), this sensitivity is weighted by the decision gradient, which reflects the realized cost of forecast-induced BESS dispatch. A feature may therefore strongly influence renewable predictions yet have limited importance for BESS operation. For importance ranking, the decision-gradient magnitude is normalized across the forecast horizon and combined with prediction sensitivity:

g¯i,topt\displaystyle\bar{g}_{i,t}^{\mathrm{opt}} ={|gi,topt|∑τ∈𝒯|gi,τopt|,‖giopt‖1>0,0,‖giopt‖1=0,\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\dfrac{|g_{i,t}^{\mathrm{opt}}|}{\displaystyle\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}}|g_{i,\tau}^{\mathrm{opt}}|},&\|g_{i}^{\mathrm{opt}}\|_{1}>0,\\[5.69054pt] 0,&\|g_{i}^{\mathrm{opt}}\|_{1}=0,\end{cases} (15a)
Si,j,tE2E\displaystyle S_{i,j,t}^{\mathrm{E2E}} =g¯i,topt​Gi,j,tpred,\displaystyle=\bar{g}_{i,t}^{\mathrm{opt}}G_{i,j,t}^{\mathrm{pred}}, (15b)
Si,jfeat\displaystyle S_{i,j}^{\mathrm{feat}} =∑t∈𝒯Si,j,tE2E,\displaystyle=\sum_{t\in\mathcal{T}}S_{i,j,t}^{\mathrm{E2E}}, (15c)
Si,ttime\displaystyle S_{i,t}^{\mathrm{time}} =g¯i,topt.\displaystyle=\bar{g}_{i,t}^{\mathrm{opt}}. (15d)

The feature score in (15c) aggregates prediction sensitivity weighted by the normalized decision gradient across the forecast horizon. The temporal score in (15d) ranks forecast periods according to their normalized decision feedback. Therefore, high prediction sensitivity does not necessarily imply high decision-oriented importance, as the latter also depends on the realized-cost sensitivity of the affected forecast periods. These magnitude-based scores are used for importance ranking.

IV-B Estimation of Decision-Oriented Importance Scores

The decision gradient is estimated using the antithetic estimator in (11b). This estimator evaluates the realized BESS cost under symmetric renewable forecast perturbations and targets the same smoothed gradient used in FC-DFL training.

For KxaiK_{\mathrm{xai}} antithetic perturbation pairs, the estimated feedback and importance scores are

g^ixai\displaystyle\widehat{g}_{i}^{\mathrm{xai}} =g^i,antiopt|K=Kxai,\displaystyle=\left.\widehat{g}_{i,\mathrm{anti}}^{\mathrm{opt}}\right|_{K=K_{\mathrm{xai}}}, (16a)
g¯^i,topt\displaystyle\widehat{\bar{g}}_{i,t}^{\mathrm{opt}} ={|g^i,txai|∑τ∈𝒯|g^i,τxai|,‖g^ixai‖1>0,0,‖g^ixai‖1=0,\displaystyle=\begin{cases}\dfrac{|\widehat{g}_{i,t}^{\mathrm{xai}}|}{\displaystyle\sum_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}}|\widehat{g}_{i,\tau}^{\mathrm{xai}}|},&\|\widehat{g}_{i}^{\mathrm{xai}}\|_{1}>0,\\[5.69054pt] 0,&\|\widehat{g}_{i}^{\mathrm{xai}}\|_{1}=0,\end{cases} (16b)
S^i,j,tE2E\displaystyle\widehat{S}_{i,j,t}^{\mathrm{E2E}} =g¯^i,topt​Gi,j,tpred.\displaystyle=\widehat{\bar{g}}_{i,t}^{\mathrm{opt}}G_{i,j,t}^{\mathrm{pred}}. (16c)

The estimated decision gradient captures the temporal sensitivity of realized BESS cost to renewable forecast changes. By weighting the predictor sensitivity with this feedback, S^i,j,tE2E\widehat{S}_{i,j,t}^{\mathrm{E2E}} identifies input features that influence forecast periods with greater importance to BESS operation. The resulting rankings are further examined through BESS reoptimization in Section IV-C.

IV-C Operational Faithfulness

The importance ranking is validated by comparing the realized BESS cost changes induced by matched perturbations of high- and low-ranked groups. All perturbed forecasts are evaluated using the same physical BESS model and realized renewable generation. For feature-level validation, the downstream cost associated with a modified predictor input is

Qi​(𝒙)=Fi​(Πℛ​[gθ​(𝒙)]),\displaystyle Q_{i}(\bm{x})=F_{i}\left(\Pi_{\mathcal{R}}\left[g_{\theta}(\bm{x})\right]\right), (17a)
Δi,Afeat=12​∑ν∈{−1,+1}|Qi​(𝒙i+ν​δx​∑j∈A𝒆j(d))−Qi​(𝒙i)|.\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \Delta_{i,A}^{\mathrm{feat}}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\nu\in\{-1,+1\}}\Big|Q_{i}\left(\bm{x}_{i}+\nu\delta_{x}\sum_{j\in A}\bm{e}_{j}^{(d)}\right)-Q_{i}(\bm{x}_{i})\Big|.\end{aligned} (17b)

High- and low-ranked renewable-history feature groups are selected by aggregating S^i,j,tE2E\widehat{S}_{i,j,t}^{\mathrm{E2E}} over the forecast horizon. All features within a group receive the same signed perturbation simultaneously. Only features permitting symmetric changes without negative historical generation are eligible. The remaining contextual inputs and exogenous regulation requirement are held fixed.

Forecast periods are ranked using the estimated temporal decision importance g¯^i,topt\widehat{\bar{g}}_{i,t}^{\mathrm{opt}}:

𝝆i0=Πℛ​(𝒓^i),\displaystyle\bm{\rho}_{i}^{0}=\Pi_{\mathcal{R}}\left(\hat{\bm{r}}_{i}\right), (18a)
Δi,Atime=12​∑ν∈{−1,+1}|Fi​(𝝆i0+ν​δr,i​∑t∈A𝒆t(T))−Fi​(𝝆i0)|.\displaystyle\begin{aligned} \Delta_{i,A}^{\mathrm{time}}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\nu\in\{-1,+1\}}\Big|F_{i}\left(\bm{\rho}_{i}^{0}+\nu\delta_{r,i}\sum_{t\in A}\bm{e}_{t}^{(T)}\right)-F_{i}(\bm{\rho}_{i}^{0})\Big|.\end{aligned} (18b)

Equal-sized high- and low-ranked groups receive matched positive and negative perturbations. For forecast-period groups, the common step δr,i\delta_{r,i} is selected so that both perturbation directions remain in ℛ\mathcal{R}. The resulting changes in realized decision cost are evaluated through BESS reoptimization. Comparing the cost changes of high- and low-ranked groups provides an empirical assessment of whether the importance scores reflect downstream BESS operation. The FC-DFL training and decision-oriented explanation procedure is summarized in Algorithm 1. The method uses the same realized BESS cost for both stages, but different estimators of the corresponding smoothed decision gradient.

V Case Studies

This section evaluates FC-DFL in terms of realized BESS regulation performance, physical operating behavior, robustness, and decision-oriented interpretability.

V-A Experimental Settings

The experiments use German hourly time-series data from Open Power System Data (OPSD) [26], including measured wind and solar generation and system load. Each sample consists of a 48-h observation history followed by a 48-h renewable forecasting and BESS dispatch horizon. The predictor uses historical renewable generation, historical load, and cyclical calendar features. The evaluation includes 560 training, 140 validation, and 100 chronologically held-out test windows with non-overlapping dispatch horizons. The test set covers March–September 2020, providing 4,800 h of measured renewable generation for out-of-sample evaluation. The exogenous balance requirement pi,tloadp_{i,t}^{\mathrm{load}} is constructed by repeating the preceding 24-h renewable profile over the dispatch horizon. Scheduled non-BESS supply is determined from the measured system load and this requirement. All methods face the same balance requirement, with renewable generation as the only uncertain quantity. A common scaling factor determined from the training data maps the measured trajectories to a study system with an average system load of 80 MW. The nominal BESS is rated at 100 MW/400 MWh, with 30 MW of retained power headroom. Charging and discharging efficiencies are 0.92, and SOC is constrained to [0.2,0.9][0.2,0.9] with initial and terminal values of 0.5. The ramp-rate limit is 60 MW/h, and the frequency coefficient is Bsys=5000B^{\mathrm{sys}}=5000 MW/Hz. The objective weights are λf=0.1\lambda_{f}=0.1 and λp=10−4\lambda_{p}=10^{-4}.

Six methods are compared under identical BESS operating conditions. Uncontrolled applies no BESS regulation, while the Realization-Aware Reference uses realized renewable generation. ERM-PTO minimizes forecast MSE, DS-DFL employs a differentiable BESS surrogate, and FC-DFL uses the proposed Gaussian-smoothed decision feedback. Empirical Scenario SD optimizes dispatch using ERM-PTO forecasts and ten empirical validation-error scenarios. The three learned predictors share the same architecture, with DS-DFL and FC-DFL initialized from ERM-PTO and selected using realized validation cost. FC-DFL uses σ0=1.3483\sigma_{0}=1.3483 MW and K=4K=4. All methods are evaluated over five independent random seeds and 100 common test windows using the same binary BESS model. The computational framework is implemented in Python using PyTorch 2.14.1 for learning, CVXPY 1.6.7 and CVXPYLayers 0.1.9 for differentiable surrogate training, and Gurobi 13.0.3 for mixed-integer BESS dispatch optimization.

V-B Forecast Accuracy and Realized Regulation Performance

FC-DFL achieves the lowest mean IAFD of 0.09529 Hz⋅\cdoth and decision regret of 97.66 among the deployable methods, as summarized in Table I. Compared with ERM-PTO, FC-DFL reduces IAFD by 6.05% and decision regret by 23.92%. A further 5.18% IAFD reduction is achieved relative to DS-DFL. These improvements demonstrate the value of training renewable forecasts according to the realized cost of their induced BESS dispatch.

The benefit of FC-DFL is also evident relative to Uncontrolled. Its mean IAFD is reduced by 3.45%, whereas ERM-PTO and DS-DFL increase IAFD by 2.77% and 1.82%, respectively. ERM-PTO achieves the lowest forecasting RMSE of 9.73 MW, but its dispatch produces a higher IAFD than Uncontrolled. This contrast highlights the importance of forecast-induced BESS decisions in determining realized regulation performance. Moreover, FC-DFL reduces BESS throughput by 61.17% relative to ERM-PTO, achieving better regulation with substantially less charging and discharging activity. Its mean IAFD is also 0.56% below Scenario SD.

The IAFD distributions over 100 held-out test windows are illustrated in Fig. 2. Each distribution is obtained by averaging over five seeds within each test window. Paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests further support the improvements achieved by FC-DFL over ERM-PTO (p=0.0066p=0.0066) and DS-DFL (p=0.0310p=0.0310). The corresponding mean IAFD reductions are 0.00614 and 0.00520 Hz⋅\cdoth, respectively. Further analysis reveals larger improvements in windows with high ERM-PTO decision regret. After grouping the test windows into quartiles according to (7d), FC-DFL achieves mean IAFD reductions of 0.00352 and 0.02210 Hz⋅\cdoth in the third and fourth quartiles, respectively. It outperforms ERM-PTO in 68% and 72% of these windows. These results indicate that the benefit of decision-focused forecasting is particularly pronounced when conventional forecasts induce costly BESS operating decisions.

V-C Forecast-Induced BESS Operation

The physical effects of forecast-induced BESS dispatch are illustrated in Fig. 3, using seed 4 and test window 42 beginning on June 5, 2020, at 22:00 UTC. The four panels trace the relationship between renewable forecasts, BESS operation, and realized frequency deviations. As illustrated in Fig. 3(a), the renewable forecasts deviate from the realized generation at different intervals, particularly during substantial changes in renewable power. These forecasts induce different BESS charging and discharging schedules under the same physical constraints.

The resulting BESS power and SOC trajectories are presented in Figs. 3(b) and (c). ERM-PTO and DS-DFL produce identical dispatch trajectories in this window. Compared with Scenario SD, FC-DFL maintains a higher SOC over much of the middle horizon, reflecting a different allocation of charging and discharging power. These differences are important because earlier BESS decisions change the stored energy available for subsequent regulation, as described by the SOC dynamics in (3f). The corresponding realized frequency deviations are illustrated in Fig. 3(d). FC-DFL achieves an IAFD of 0.07427 Hz⋅\cdoth, representing a 47.37% reduction relative to Uncontrolled (0.14112 Hz⋅\cdoth). Further IAFD reductions of 4.69% and 8.57% are obtained relative to ERM-PTO/DS-DFL and Scenario SD, respectively. Meanwhile, FC-DFL requires 388.87 MWh of BESS throughput, compared with 437.51 MWh for ERM-PTO/DS-DFL. The results illustrate how forecast-induced BESS dispatch and intertemporal SOC evolution affect realized regulation performance.

V-D Robustness Across BESS and Renewable Conditions

The robustness of FC-DFL is evaluated under different BESS operating conditions. The energy capacity is varied from 200 to 600 MWh, and the ramp-rate limit from 30 to 90 MW/h. The learned predictors remain fixed, while BESS dispatch is reoptimized for each configuration. Across all tested configurations, FC-DFL achieves the lowest mean IAFD among the deployable methods, as illustrated in Figs. 4(a) and (b). Relative to ERM-PTO, the IAFD reduction remains between 6.05% and 6.10% for different energy capacities and between 5.40% and 6.13% for different ramp-rate limits. These results demonstrate that the improvement is maintained across the tested BESS operating conditions.

Renewable forecast-error stress is further examined using constructed renewable realizations based on ERM-PTO forecasts and empirical validation-error trajectories scaled by α∈{0.5,1.0,1.5}\alpha\in\{0.5,1.0,1.5\}. For each seed and test window, the same error trajectory is scaled across the three stress levels. The learned predictors and exogenous balance requirement remain unchanged. Under these conditions, FC-DFL consistently achieves lower IAFD and decision regret than ERM-PTO and DS-DFL, as presented in Figs. 4(c) and (d). The IAFD reductions relative to ERM-PTO reach 4.36%, 6.74%, and 6.30% at the three stress levels, respectively. Corresponding reductions in decision regret range from 21.9% to 26.3%. Together, these results demonstrate that FC-DFL maintains its regulation advantage across the tested BESS configurations and renewable forecast-error conditions.

V-E Decision-Oriented Importance and Operational Faithfulness

The XAI evaluation considers 50 selected seed-window cases, including 45 with nonzero decision feedback. The antithetic estimator uses Kxai=64K_{\mathrm{xai}}=64, with prediction sensitivities computed for standardized inputs. The resulting feature-time importance scores in (16c) are illustrated in Fig. 5(a). Among the 98 predictor inputs, the 1-h and 2-h renewable-history lags receive the highest aggregate importance, followed by the day-of-year features. The importance also varies across forecast periods, indicating that the influence of an input on BESS operation depends on the timing of its forecast contribution.

A clear distinction emerges between prediction sensitivity and decision-oriented importance. For temporal comparison, prediction sensitivity is aggregated across input features as ∑jGi,j,tpred\sum_{j}G_{i,j,t}^{\mathrm{pred}} and compared with the estimated temporal decision importance g¯^i,topt\widehat{\bar{g}}_{i,t}^{\mathrm{opt}}. As reported in Table II, the mean Spearman correlation between their temporal rankings is only 0.019, with an average top-5 overlap of 0.67 periods. The five highest-ranked decision periods account for 28.7% of the total decision weight, compared with 10.4% under uniform weighting. These results highlight the difference between forecast periods sensitive to predictor inputs and those important to realized BESS operation. Operational faithfulness is further examined through matched perturbations and exact BESS reoptimization, following (17) and (18). High- and low-ranked renewable-history groups each contain five eligible features, perturbed by 0.1 training standard deviation. Forecast-period groups contain five periods with matched feasible perturbations of up to 1 MW. The resulting changes in realized decision cost are evaluated under the same renewable realization.

The operational relevance of the importance rankings is evaluated in Fig. 5(b) and Table II. High-ranked renewable-history groups produce a mean |Δ​F||\Delta F| of 5.40, compared with 3.76 for low-ranked groups, representing a 1.44-fold difference. The distinction is more pronounced for forecast periods, where high-ranked groups produce 2.84 times the realized cost change of low-ranked groups (3.72 versus 1.31). Both differences are statistically significant under paired Wilcoxon signed-rank tests. The larger realized cost changes for high-ranked groups support the operational relevance of the proposed importance rankings. Unlike prediction sensitivity alone, the decision-oriented importance scores account for the sensitivity of realized BESS cost to forecast changes. The matched perturbation results further demonstrate that the decision feedback used for FC-DFL training also provides a basis for interpreting the operating consequences of renewable forecasts.

V-F Sensitivity to Smoothing Radius and Perturbation Budget

The Gaussian smoothing radius σ\sigma and perturbation budget KK govern the estimation of decision feedback in (11a). The smoothing radius determines the scale of renewable forecast perturbations used to evaluate realized BESS cost, while KK controls the number of perturbation directions used for each gradient estimate. Their effects are evaluated by varying one parameter at a time around the nominal setting (σ0,K)=(1.3483​MW,4)(\sigma_{0},K)=(1.3483\ \mathrm{MW},4). Unlike the BESS operating-limit tests in Section V-D, these experiments retain the same physical BESS constraints and realized-cost evaluation. They examine the influence of gradient-estimation settings on the decision feedback used for renewable predictor training.

With K=4K=4, the mean IAFD remains between 0.09529 and 0.09554 Hz⋅\cdoth as σ/σ0\sigma/\sigma_{0} varies from 0.5 to 2.0. The nominal smoothing radius achieves the lowest decision regret of 97.66 among these three settings, compared with 98.84 and 98.90 at the smaller and larger radii, respectively. The small differences indicate that the realized regulation performance is relatively insensitive to the smoothing radius within the examined range. The influence of the perturbation budget is examined at σ=σ0\sigma=\sigma_{0}. Increasing KK from 2 to 8 does not produce a consistent improvement in regulation performance. As reported in Table III, the mean IAFD varies from 0.09527 to 0.09540 Hz⋅\cdoth, while the offline training time increases from 135.82 to 332.76 s. Thus, a larger perturbation budget increases computational effort without a corresponding reduction in realized IAFD under the tested settings.

Across all five configurations, FC-DFL maintains an IAFD reduction of 5.80%–6.07% relative to ERM-PTO, as illustrated in Fig. 6. These results demonstrate that the regulation benefits of FC-DFL are maintained under different smoothing radii and perturbation budgets, supporting the numerical robustness of the proposed decision-feedback training.

VI Conclusion

This paper developed Frequency-Calibrated Decision-Focused Learning (FC-DFL) to align renewable forecasting with the operational objectives of constrained BESS dispatch. FC-DFL leverages feedback from the realized outcomes of forecast-driven BESS dispatch to guide predictor training, enabling forecasts to be optimized for their downstream operational results. Building on the same decision feedback, we further developed a decision-oriented XAI method that combines it with prediction sensitivity to identify the forecasting inputs and periods most relevant to BESS dispatch. Case studies using German wind and solar data demonstrated that FC-DFL reduced the integrated absolute frequency-deviation metric by 6.05% and decision regret by 23.92% compared with accuracy-based predict-then-optimize approach. BESS energy throughput was also reduced by 61.17%. The XAI analysis further revealed that high-ranked forecast periods produced mean absolute realized decision-cost changes 2.84 times those of low-ranked periods, supporting the operational relevance of the proposed importance rankings. These findings highlight the importance of learning from downstream decision-making results in renewable forecasting. The proposed method can support both predictor training and identify the forecasting information that matters more to BESS operation. Future work will extend FC-DFL to network-constrained BESS operation and dynamic frequency-response models.
